lines.text: Any lord may raise to knighthood any commoner who holds a bridge for the realm. I found that sentence the night Hask came to measure us. I'd been waiting for a bridge ever since.
Now I had two bridges, and three people who had held them. The ice bridge over the gorge, where Wren and Garrow stopped nine Hounds. And the mill bridge, where Tobin held thirty men until dawn.
So on the coldest morning of the year, in front of the whole north, I had the law read aloud in the square. Not by a herald. By my wards.
Six children who had learned their letters on a steamed-up window. They had practised for three days, and argued about who got the long words for four.
Any lord may raise to knighthood any commoner...
...who holds a bridge, for the realm.
Their reading was slow. Every word was right. Half the square was crying, and the other half said it was the wind.
This is a mockery! Knighthood is for blood and rings! A smith? A hunter's girl? A one-eyed Skeld deserter?
My smith has four rings, Lord Hollis. Your captain has two. I checked.
And I've seen the girl shoot, Hollis. If you'd like a demonstration, go and stand by that apple tree.
The law is the law, my lords. You all signed a Compact built on it. Lord Lucan simply reads it more carefully than you do.
I don't own a sword. I've never been able to lift one properly. So I knighted them with the only weapon in Greyhollow that everyone respects. Granny's axe.
Mind the edge, my lord. It's still mine.
Wren knelt first. She looked furious about it. I touched the flat of the axe to each shoulder.
Rise, Sir Wren of Greyhollow.
If anyone calls me Sir Wren, I'll shoot them.
Garrow knelt beside his daughter, and said nothing at all, and didn't need to. Then Tobin knelt, and a flagstone cracked under his knee.
Sorry, my lord. I'll fix that. Sir Tobin will fix that.
Knights of clay. That's all they are. Farmers' knights, made of mud.

He meant it as an insult. By the end of the week, every one of Wren's archers had painted a stripe of clay across their shield. They called themselves the Clay Knights, and they meant it as a promise.
And I understood, at last, why that clause was in the Charter. Three hundred years ago, a hollow-born king had farmers growing rings too. He needed a way to make them knights.
My lord. Since I'm a knight now. That old book of my grandfather's. I think I've finally read the last page.
The Lord Who Measured Zero. Chapter one hundred and twenty-three, coming soon.
